title: The Scientific Method: How Knowledge Is Built and Tested
paragraphs: Science is often misunderstood as a collection of facts — a body of fixed knowledge about the world that students memorise and experts possess. In reality, science is better understood as a process: a set of methods for investigating the natural world, testing ideas against evidence, and gradually refining our understanding over time. This process is imperfect, slow, and sometimes frustrating — but it is also the most reliable tool humanity has developed for distinguishing what is true from what merely seems to be true.

At the heart of the scientific method is the concept of the hypothesis — a provisional explanation of an observed phenomenon that can be tested. A good scientific hypothesis makes specific, measurable predictions: if the hypothesis is correct, then certain things should be observable under certain conditions. The scientist then designs an experiment to test these predictions. If the results match the predictions, the hypothesis is supported; if they do not, the hypothesis must be revised or rejected. This cycle of hypothesis, test, and revision is the engine of scientific progress.

A critical feature of good experimental design is the control of variables. In any real-world situation, many factors might influence the outcome of an experiment. If a scientist wants to know whether a particular drug reduces blood pressure, they need to ensure that all other factors — the patients' diet, exercise, stress levels, and other medications — are kept as constant as possible between the test group (those receiving the drug) and the control group (those receiving a placebo). The more carefully variables are controlled, the more confident the scientist can be that any observed effect is genuinely caused by the factor being tested.

Replication is another cornerstone of scientific knowledge. A single experiment, however carefully designed, might produce results due to chance, error, or undetected confounding factors. Only when an experiment is successfully repeated by independent researchers — using different samples, different equipment, and sometimes different methodologies — does its result begin to qualify as reliable knowledge. The failure to replicate many widely-cited findings in psychology and medicine, known as the "replication crisis," has prompted significant reflection on research practices and publication standards across the sciences.

Peer review — the process by which scientific papers are evaluated by other experts in the field before publication — serves as the primary quality-control mechanism of academic science. Peer reviewers scrutinise the methodology, statistics, and interpretations of submitted papers, and can request revisions, additional experiments, or reject papers outright. While peer review is far from perfect — reviewers can miss flaws, and publication bias can distort what gets published — it represents a significant improvement over the alternative of unreviewed publishing.

One of the most important concepts in understanding science is the distinction between a hypothesis, a theory, and a law. In everyday language, "theory" often means a guess or speculation. In science, a theory is something much stronger: it is a well-substantiated explanation of a set of phenomena, supported by a large body of evidence from multiple independent lines of inquiry. The theory of evolution, the germ theory of disease, the theory of relativity — these are not guesses. They are the most thoroughly tested and supported explanations we have for the phenomena they describe.

Science is also a human activity, conducted by people with careers, interests, biases, and limited resources. It is important to understand that scientists are not perfectly objective truth-machines. They can be motivated by ambition, institutional pressures, or the desire to defend positions they have publicly committed to. This is why the social institutions of science — peer review, replication, the practice of open data and transparent methodology — are so important. They provide mechanisms for self-correction that can, over time, overcome the biases of individual researchers and communities.

vocab.definition: a provisional, testable explanation for an observed phenomenon
vocab.example: "A good hypothesis makes specific, measurable predictions that can be tested."

vocab.definition: the repetition of an experiment by independent researchers to verify its results
vocab.example: "Only when an experiment is successfully replicated does its result qualify as reliable knowledge."

vocab.definition: relating to an uncontrolled variable that affects experimental results
vocab.example: "Confounding factors can make it appear that a drug works when it does not."
